newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Proton takes control of Lotus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Proton takes control of Lotus.

text.p: Malaysia's Proton vehicle manufacturer said on Wednesday it had bought an 80 percent interest in Lotus Group, the troubled British sports car company.

Yahaya Ahmad, chairman of Proton's parent DRB-HICOM and one of Malaysia's most influential businessmen, is taking a 16.25 percent personal stake in Lotus Group International, alongside Proton's 63.75 percent interest, Proton said.

"Lotus is a legend -- it's a name that conjures excitement all over the world. It gives Proton an instant capacity to have products in the showrooms that have the Lotus image," Yahaya told a news conference at Lotus' factory in eastern England. Payment is 51 million pounds ($83 million) plus a loan of 13 million pounds to cover working capital.

Proton said in a statement that the change in ownership will not affect the way that the company's businesses are managed, including Lotus Engineering, which will continue to pursue its role as a leading independent supplier of design engineering services and technology to automotive and industrial clients.
The deal ends months of uncertainty for the British firm, whose owner, Italian entrepreneur Romano Artioli, has been seeking a major investor for most of this year.
Yahaya said Proton planned an immediate increase in production of Lotus' Elise sports car in England and would add production capacity in Malaysia.
"With our contribution we can expand Lotus production here...we will expand capacity immediately," he said.

The company hoped to bring production up to 10 cars per day from the current five, and additional capacity to serve Far Eastern markets would be added at Proton plants in Malaysia to give total Elise production capacity of about 5,000 cars per year.
Outgoing chairman Artioli told reporters, "I think I have done my part to ensure that Lotus can now expand its activities."
He said the deal was just three pages long and he liked it because it secured Lotus' three key interest in sports car making, engineering consultancy and motor racing.
Both men stressed the deal would preserve Lotus' independence as a provider of consultancy services to international motor manufacturers.
Yahaya said, "It must remain independent -- we are not going to subsidise Lotus."
Artioli owned Lotus via the Luxembourg-registered Bugatti International SA group, which in turn is the parent of the Italian car company Bugatti Automobili which went into receivership last year.

Started by motor racing engineer Colin Chapman in the early 1950s, Lotus was once a leading name in Grand Prix racing, winning world championships with drivers Graham Hill, Jim Clark, Jochen Rindt, Emerson Fittipaldi and Mario Andretti.
Cars produced by the company included the Lotus Seven, the Lotus Elan, the Elite and its new model, the Elise.
Lotus was taken over by General Motors in 1986, and then piled up losses of 50 million pounds ($75 million) in the five years before its sale in 1993 to Bugatti International. ($1=.6165 Pound)
